question: Find where request validation happens and explain how invalid requests are rejected.
answer:
- Validation is implemented in the validate-request middleware and applied in routes. The middleware is defined in src/middleware/validate-request.js and uses a schema to parse the request part, e.g., body or params. If parsing fails, it throws an ApplicationError with 400 and a details payload. Evidence: src/middleware/validate-request.js:3-9, 11-13. These lines show safeParse, 400 error creation, and storing validated data on request.validated. Also routes wire it up (see product routes). Evidence: src/routes/product-routes.js:11, 12, 14-20. 

- The routes apply the validator to various endpoints, ensuring inputs are validated before controllers run. For example, product routes use validateRequest(productQuerySchema, 'query'), validateRequest(identifierParametersSchema, 'params'), etc. Evidence: src/routes/product-routes.js:11-20.

- Invalid input results in an error thrown by the validator. The thrown error is an instance of ApplicationError with statusCode 400 and a validation-specific code/message, plus a details array describing issues. Evidence: src/middleware/validate-request.js:7-9.

- The error is handled by the centralized error handling middleware registered in the application, which formats and returns a JSON error response. Evidence that error handling is wired: src/app.js lines 76-78 show the error route not-found and error handler being added; in server startup, createErrorHandler(logger) is used to handle errors. Evidence: src/app.js:76-78.

- The ApplicationError class defines the structure used for validation errors, including statusCode, code, message, and optional details. This is the same type used by the validator. Evidence: src/errors/application-error.js:1-8.

- The HTTP response for a validation failure is a JSON object containing an error block with code, message, and optional details, plus the requestId. Evidence: src/middleware/error-handler.js:27-33. The 400 status is set on applicationError by the validator and preserved through the error handler. Evidence: src/middleware/validate-request.js:7-9, and src/middleware/error-handler.js:27-33.

question: Where is the Express application created, and where does it start listening?
answer:
- The Express application instance is created inside src/app.js as part of the createApplication function, where express() is called to build the app (see src/app.js:44).  
  Evidence: src/app.js:44

- The application is created by calling createApplication (imported from ./app.js) in src/server.js, and then the server starts listening on the configured port with application.listen(...): see src/server.js:8-11.  
  Evidence: src/server.js:8-11

- The listen call uses the port from the configuration and logs when the server has started (src/server.js:9-11).  
  Evidence: src/server.js:9-11

question: Which endpoints are public and which require authentication?
answer:
- Public: user registration and login endpoints (no authentication required). See authentication routes: POST /api/v1/auth/register and POST /api/v1/auth/login. Evidence: src/routes/authentication-routes.js:7-8. Also note logout endpoints require auth (see next item) so registration/login are the public auth entry points. src/routes/authentication-routes.js:9-10 for logout endpoints.

  - src/routes/authentication-routes.js:7-8
  - src/routes/authentication-routes.js:9-10

- Public: product listing and product retrieval endpoints (no authentication required). Evidence: GET /api/v1/products/ and GET /api/v1/products/:identifier are defined without an authentication middleware. src/routes/product-routes.js:11-12. 

  - src/routes/product-routes.js:11-12

- Public: health check endpoints (alive/ready) are accessible without authentication. Evidence: src/app.js defines /health/live and /health/ready before any authentication middleware is applied. src/app.js:51-54.

  - src/app.js:51-54

- Requires authentication: logout actions require an authenticated user. Evidence: authentication routes include POST /logout and POST /logout-all guarded by authenticateRequest. src/routes/authentication-routes.js:9-10.

  - src/routes/authentication-routes.js:9-10

- Requires authentication: user-related endpoints are all behind authentication for the /api/v1/users router. Evidence: router.use(authenticateRequest); then GET /me, PATCH /me, POST /me/password, POST /me/deactivate. src/routes/user-routes.js:7-11.

  - src/routes/user-routes.js:7-12

- Requires authentication (and permissions): all product mutation routes and admin/order routes require authentication (and specific permissions where applicable). Evidence:
  - Product mutations: router.use(authenticateRequest, requirePermission('products:manage')) before POST/PATCH/stock-adjustments/archive. src/routes/product-routes.js:13-20.
  - Administration: router.use(authenticateRequest) before admin endpoints; and per-endpoint permissions for users/audit/metrics. src/routes/administration-routes.js:8-12.
  - Orders: router.use(authenticateRequest); then per-route permission checks like orders:read-own, orders:create, etc. src/routes/order-routes.js:11-20.

  - src/routes/product-routes.js:13-20
  - src/routes/administration-routes.js:8-12
  - src/routes/order-routes.js:11-20

question: Which database tables or migrations store orders?
answer:
- There are no database tables or migrations for orders in this codebase—the storage is in-memory. See the memory-backed repositories where orders are defined as a Map: src/repositories/memory-repositories.js:8. The orders repository is exposed as repositories.orders: src/repositories/memory-repositories.js:33.
- When an order is created, the service saves it to the in-memory orders store: src/services/order-service.js:101 (repositories.orders.save(order)).
